page.title: tinyactors: like SQLite, but for actors
page.description: tinyactors runs each entity as a statechart actor inside your own Node.js, Python, browser or C process: one place to look, small enough to inspect, and checkable by a computer.

hero.headline: Stateful systems you can reason about
hero.lede: An order's logic ends up spread over a queue, a worker, a cron job and three status columns, and nobody owns it. tinyactors puts it in one statechart, run by an actor inside your own process. Like SQLite, but for actors.

section.heading: The chart decides, your code acts
section.p: The order actor keeps its cart in its data model, and its chart decides what each event means. When the payment service cannot be reached, the order tries again on its own.

The chart reaches the world only by sending events to an I/O processor, an object your program gives the host. This program's payment service fails the first charge, and the order retries a second later:

section.heading: One process you can reason about
section.p: A web server, a queue, a worker and a cron job each hold part of an order. To know what it does next, you read all four.
A tinyactors host runs inside your program. There's no server to operate, each actor handles one event at a time, and its whole behavior is one chart.

item.text: Node.js and Bun, Python, the browser and C, each a package over the same C core.
One core behind every package, and every package runs the W3C SCXML tests.
A crash stops every actor in the process. When to use tinyactors says what comes back and when to choose something else.

section.heading: Small enough to see every actor
section.p: An actor takes about half a kilobyte, so a request, a connection or an order can each be one. Millions fit in one process, and your code can look at any of them.

item.text: its states, its variables, its queue and its pending timers, while it runs.
two million actors, 1000 of them in memory, make a 165 MB snapshot that another process restores.
two colonies of ants in your browser tab, every ant and queen an actor.

section.heading: Behavior a computer can check
section.p: An Erlang or Akka actor runs any code you give it. A tinyactors actor runs a W3C SCXML chart, with every state and transition written down.
The same chart runs in your process and in a simulation, where a simulated clock runs its timeouts in milliseconds (testing your charts).

section.heading: Kill your unit tests
section.p: A unit test checks one run you wrote down. A property is a rule, like "never charge a card more than three times", checked on runs a program generates.

section.heading: Local reasoning for agents
section.p: An agent writes an actor from the events entering and leaving it, not from the whole system. Every effect leaves the chart as an event your code performs, so reviewing its change means reading one file.
In CI, tinyactors check, lint and diff catch a misspelt event and show what behavior a change moved (CI checks).

section.heading: Your infrastructure, not ours
section.p: Hosted actor platforms decide where your code runs, where its state lives and what each step costs. tinyactors decides none of that: your program already did.

item.text: A chart asks for outside work by sending an event to an object of yours, which answers with another. Tests answer instead of a real service.
Waiting actors leave memory for the store you already run: two million ran with at most 1000 in memory.

term.link: A journal if you want one

item.text: Record every input, and one loop rebuilds every actor after a crash.
An actor sends to an actor in another process by its address, over the transport you choose.

section.heading: Change behavior while it runs
section.p: An order lives for days, and your rules change in the middle. Add the chart's new version to the running process: new orders start on it, and running ones keep the state they reached.

item.text: moves each running actor to the new version at a stable point, with its states, queue and timers.

section.heading: Conquer complexity
section.p: A team chat's hard state is who is in each room and who is online. The five-step tutorial puts each part of that state in an actor:

item.text: Two joins at the same moment can overwrite each other in a shared member list. A room actor handles one event at a time, so its member list keeps every join.
A user who stops being active sends no event, so nothing marks them as away. The user's chart restarts a timer on each activity and marks the user away after 300 seconds.

Most users are idle, and each one's data takes memory as long as it stays loaded. An idle user's actor is saved to a store and loaded again on its next event: a thousand users ran with fifty in memory.

section.heading: When to choose something else
section.p: When your application must run on many machines at once, with placement and failover handled for you, the infrastructure is the product. Then a platform built for that fits better.

item.term: Is one process a single point of failure?
item.text: Yes: a crash stops every actor in it. What comes back is what your program saved: hibernated actors in your store, the last snapshot and a journal if you keep one.
SCXML is a W3C standard, so a chart isn't tied to one library or language. The same chart runs in Node.js, Python, a browser and C (tinyactors compared with XState).

item.term: Do I have to write XML?
item.text: A chart is an SCXML document, and the expressions in it are JavaScript. The tinyactors command draws it, checks it and runs it before your program does.

item.term: Is anyone running this in production?
item.text: tinyactors is at version 0.x and still changes its API in minor releases. What backs it: the W3C SCXML suite in every package, and programs that take two million actors through hibernation, migration and snapshots (performance).

item.term: Will an agent write good charts?
item.text: An agent writes one chart from the events it takes and sends, and the command line catches mistakes such as a misspelt event in CI (build with a coding agent).
